title: Zero Registered Slaughterhouses: Vietnam's Dog Meat Trade Has No Rules
excerpt: Vietnam has no registered dog meat slaughterhouses — a total enforcement vacuum that puts public health at serious risk.
body_html:
In Vietnam, an estimated 5 million dogs are killed for meat every year. Yet there is not a single registered, inspected, or regulated slaughterhouse in the entire country to handle them. That is not a minor compliance gap — it is the complete absence of a food safety framework for an industry operating at enormous scale. No veterinary oversight. No hygiene standards. No traceability. Every step of the supply chain, from theft or capture to slaughter and sale, happens entirely outside the law.

The consequences for public health are direct and measurable. Unregulated dog slaughter is a documented vector for rabies transmission — the movement of live dogs across provinces spreads the virus into areas that would otherwise be clear. Workers who handle animals in uncontrolled conditions face acute exposure risk. Consumers face contamination from E. coli and Salmonella, pathogens that regulated meat processing is specifically designed to eliminate. When there are no inspections, there are no safeguards — and when there are no safeguards, people get sick.

Other countries have demonstrated that ending the dog meat trade produces measurable public health improvements. South Korea, which has moved to phase out the industry through formal legislation, saw sustained pressure from its own public health authorities who cited disease risk as a primary driver. The Philippines banned the trade in 1998, and enforcement — however imperfect — created clear lines of accountability that unregulated markets simply cannot provide. The common thread in every successful case is that the change was framed as a public health and governance issue, not only an animal welfare question. Regulation, or the lack of it, is the core problem.

Crucially, this is not an agenda being imposed from outside. A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese people support ending the dog meat trade. That supermajority includes urban residents, younger generations, and local authorities in cities like Hanoi and Hoi An that have already issued voluntary phase-out guidance. The will for change is domestic, democratic, and decisive. What is missing is a national regulatory framework that matches the values the Vietnamese public has already clearly expressed.

Ending the dog meat trade in Vietnam is, at its foundation, a question of governance. A food industry that operates with zero registered facilities, zero veterinary checks, and zero traceability cannot be made safe — it can only be ended. The legal infrastructure, the public support, and the public health rationale all point in the same direction. Vietnam has the opportunity to close this enforcement gap permanently, protect its citizens from preventable disease, and align national policy with what 95% of its own people already want. Sign the petition and add your voice to theirs.
